summary: Describes the architecture of the Internet Relay Chat (IRC) protocol and the roles of its components such as clients, servers and channels. Other documents give the detailed protocol rules. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: IRC connects servers in a tree and connects clients to those servers. Servers locate clients, host channels, and relay messages across the network.

questions: how does internet relay chat work
why does irc use a spanning tree
how are messages relayed in irc
subtitle: The IRC network model: servers form a tree, while clients connect at its edges.

tldr.problem: IRC needed an updated description of its architecture and the roles of servers, clients, and channels.
tldr.mechanism: IRC servers connect in a spanning tree, track clients and channels, and relay messages between clients; clients do not communicate directly.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo updates RFC 1459 and describes architectural limits involving scalability, reliability, congestion, and privacy.

today: RFC 2810 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 2810 itself.

sections.title: Servers and Clients
sections.content:
Internet Relay Chat (IRC) is a protocol for text-based conferencing. RFC 2810 describes its architecture and updates RFC 1459; other documents define detailed rules for communication between components.

A server is the backbone of an IRC network and accepts connections from clients and other servers. Clients are either user programs for interactive chat or service programs that perform automated tasks.
sections.plainLanguage: IRC servers connect the network's components and relay messages. Clients connect to servers, either for people to chat or for automated services.

sections.title: A Tree of Servers and Hosted Channels
sections.content:
An IRC network consists of servers connected as a spanning tree. A single server can form the simplest network. The protocol provides no direct client-to-client communication; servers relay all client messages.

Servers locate clients by their registered labels and host channels. A channel is a named group of one or more users who receive messages sent to that channel.
sections.plainLanguage: IRC servers connect without loops, and clients attach to servers. A client sends a message through the servers rather than directly to another client.

sections.title: How IRC Delivers Messages
sections.content:
For one-to-one communication, servers send a message along the tree to the destination client. For a channel message, the network sends it only to servers that support users on that channel, and each server forwards it over each needed local link once.

Clients may also send to host or server masks, or provide a list of targets. A list is less efficient because the server sends separate copies and may not check for duplicates. State-changing messages are generally sent to all servers to keep their information consistent.
sections.plainLanguage: A private message follows the route through servers to one client. A channel message reaches servers with channel members, and each server delivers it locally.

sections.title: Architectural Problems
sections.content:
The memo identifies scalability as a problem because each server must know about all servers, clients, and channels and must receive updates when that state changes. The tree also makes each server-to-server link a point of failure.

Congestion can worsen when a link fails and servers reconnect. The memo strongly recommends that servers not reconnect automatically too quickly. It also identifies privacy concerns because servers hold information about network entities and channels.
sections.plainLanguage: Every server must keep extensive information about the network. This limits growth, makes links important failure points, and raises privacy concerns.

sections.title: Security and Companion Protocols
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says that, apart from the privacy concerns already noted, security is believed to be irrelevant to this architecture document.

The memo points readers to separate documents for the client protocol, server protocol, and channel management. Those documents describe the detailed protocol rules that this architecture overview does not provide.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo focuses on architecture and does not discuss security beyond its privacy concerns. Separate RFCs describe client, server, and channel-management rules.
